 Massachusetts wants to stop changing the clocks. It needs at least 2 other states to agree.
 The proposal would put Massachusetts on year-round Atlantic time, but at least two neighboring states would also have to agree to make the switch.
 A jogger passes a gazebo in Old Harbor Park at dawn, in Boston, MA on October 21, 2026. Daylight saving time will end on Sunday, November 1, 2026. (Craig F. Walker/Globe Staff) 
 By Annie Jonas 
 November 2, 2026 | 1:33 PM

 A day after Americans set their clocks back an hour, Massachusetts lawmakers took another step toward making it the last time residents have to do so. 
 The Senate Committee on Rules voted 5-0 on Thursday, Oct. 29, to give initial approval to a bill ( S. 2157 ) that would move Massachusetts to the Atlantic time zone year-round. The change would put the state one hour ahead of its current Eastern time zone, giving residents an extra hour of evening daylight during winter — similar to what they would experience under year-round daylight saving time.
 But Massachusetts couldn’t make the change alone. The bill would take effect only if at least two neighboring states — New Hampshire, Vermont, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New York, or Maine — also agreed to switch to the Atlantic time zone. The governor would then have to seek approval from the U.S. Department of Transportation, which as federal authority over time zones.
 Advertisement: And the proposal still has several steps to clear before it could become law.
 The Oct. 29 vote did not amount to final Senate approval. Instead, senators voted to order the bill to a “third reading,” a procedural step that sends it through a final proofreading before it returns to the full Senate for further debate and consideration. The Senate would still need to pass the bill, followed by the House of Representatives and the governor’s approval.
 In a news release, Senate President Karen Spilka called changing the clocks a “ridiculous seasonal dance” that disrupts people’s sleep. She said having one permanent time would be better for residents’ health and make roads safer.
 Advertisement: “I hear about this often from constituents who are tired of this outdated relic of the 20th century. Permanently establishing a single time system would improve our health and even make our roads safer,” she said in the release.
 Sen. John Keenan, a Quincy Democrat, who sponsored the bill, cited additional potential benefits, including lowering the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and car accidents, as well as increased workplace productivity.
